pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** What Plants Need to Thrive (comparing requirements)

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y3 'Plants'):** 'explore the requirements of plants for life and growth (air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow) and how they vary from plant to plant.' Two demands: the FULL set of five requirements (adding air, nutrients-from-soil and room to the Y2 water/light/warmth), and that requirements VARY between plants.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-LS2-1 / K-LS1-1):** the US anchors plant needs at '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1]' (2-LS2-1); the fuller five-factor list and the 'varies plant to plant' comparison is a UK-specific KS2 elaboration.

- **Operational details:** This extends the Y2 'water, light, warmth' to the Y3 FIVE: air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow. Two of these are newly non-obvious to children — AIR (plants need it too, not just animals) and ROOM/space (crowded plants compete and grow poorly) — so give them deliberate attention. The distinctive Y3 move is COMPARISON: different plants need different AMOUNTS (a cactus thrives on little water; a fern needs lots and shade), so 'requirements vary from plant to plant' — this pre-empts a one-size-fits-all rule and connects to habitat/adaptation. Teach through comparative fair tests (vary one factor, including crowding and nutrients, across plant types) and through matching plants to the conditions they prefer. Note carefully: 'nutrients from soil' are minerals for health, NOT the plant's food/mass source — keep that door open for the later 'plants make their own food / mass from air & water' idea; don't let 'nutrients from soil' harden into 'plants eat soil'.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B. The child lists the five requirements (including the easily-missed air and room), predicts the effect of removing/limiting one, and — the Y3 discriminator — explains that different plants need different amounts (e.g. cactus vs fern water needs), matching a plant to suitable conditions.
bestPractices: Explicitly add and dwell on the two non-obvious requirements — AIR (plants need it as well as animals) and ROOM to grow (overcrowding starves plants of light/water/space) — which children routinely omit.
Centre the Y3 upgrade on COMPARISON: different plants need different amounts (cactus vs fern), so requirements vary — use matching/sorting of plants to preferred conditions.
Run comparative fair tests that include the new variables (crowding, nutrient-poor vs rich) not just water/light, changing one factor at a time.
Frame 'nutrients from soil' as minerals for HEALTH, not as the plant's food or mass — avoid cementing 'plants eat soil' (bridge to the air/water idea later).
Link 'requirements vary' to habitat — a plant thrives where its needs are met — seeding adaptation without over-reaching.
keyRepresentations: A five-icon requirements set (air, light, water, nutrients, room) as condition labels.
A plant–conditions matching board (cactus → dry/bright; fern → damp/shady) showing needs vary.
A crowding comparison: seedlings sown dense vs spaced, showing competition for room.
A comparative fair-test layout varying one factor across two plant types.
commonMisconceptions: Omitting air and room to grow — listing only water and light as plant needs.
Assuming all plants need identical conditions/amounts (watering a cactus like a fern).
Believing plants 'eat' soil / that soil nutrients are the plant's food and the source of its mass (should be minerals-for-health only at this stage).
Thinking more of any requirement is always better (over-watering, no limit to fertiliser).
Not recognising that overcrowding harms plants (seeing 'more plants together' as fine).
Treating light as optional if the plant is watered (carryover from the Y2 misconception).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, extend the earlier 'water, light, warmth' idea to the full set of five plant requirements — air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow — with deliberate attention to the two children routinely omit: AIR (plants need it too, not just animals) and ROOM/space (crowded plants compete and grow poorly). The distinctive Year-3 move is COMPARISON: different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements (a cactus thrives on little water; a fern needs lots and shade), so 'requirements vary from plant to plant'. Teach through comparative fair tests (vary one factor, including crowding and nutrients, across plant types) and by matching plants to the conditions they prefer, linking this to habitat/adaptation. Keep 'nutrients from soil' as minerals for health, not the plant's food or source of mass, so the later 'plants make their own food from air and water' idea stays open.

activities.title: Plant compare-lab: same care, different outcomes
feedback: If a learner predicts both plants thrive with lots of water, show the over-watered cactus yellowing/rotting: the right AMOUNT matters and it differs by plant — more isn't always better.
If a learner says all plants need identical amounts, compare a desert home to a forest floor: the plants are suited to different conditions, so their needs differ in amount.

If a learner lists only water and light, crowd seedlings in one pot so they visibly compete for space, light, water and nutrients and tend to grow weaker or smaller — room to grow and nutrients are needs too; and prompt that plants also need air.
activities.rationale: The Year-3 heart is comparison, and two new factors (air, room) are easier to grasp when their effects are seen. An interactive compare-lab gives deterministic, time-lapsed outcomes a child can produce quickly, so 'different plants need different amounts' becomes a result they generate rather than a rule they are told; a live cactus and fern ground the comparison in real plants. Real-plant results should be framed as expected tendencies, since living-plant outcomes are not guaranteed. The crowding comparison makes the easily-missed 'room to grow' requirement concrete.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the requirements of plants for life and growth (air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow) and how they vary from plant to plant'.
NGSS anchors plant needs at '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-LS2-1]' (2-LS2-1); the fuller five-factor list and vary-plant-to-plant comparison is a UK KS2 elaboration.
Children routinely omit air and room-to-grow from plant needs and treat soil nutrients as the plant's food; instruction should name the full set and keep 'nutrients from soil' as minerals-for-health.
learnerActions: Use an interactive compare-lab (a simulated side-by-side setup) to grow a cactus and a fern together, with dials for water, light, nutrients and how tightly each is planted, plus an air toggle, so you can adjust conditions and time-lapse growth; pair this with a real cactus and fern on the windowsill to ground the comparison in living plants you tend.
Set each plant's conditions and compare how each responds to the same settings.

Predict before observing, and say why: what will happen to each plant if you turn BOTH plants' water up high? Keep a second cactus and fern on low water to compare against. Then watch what happens — in the compare-lab the high-water fern flourishes while the high-water cactus yellows and rots, unlike the low-water cactus (with real plants, treat this as the expected tendency over a fortnight, not a guaranteed result).
State in your own words why the SAME generous watering helps one plant and harms the other.

Crowd several seedlings of the same kind tightly together and compare them with well-spaced seedlings given the same water and light, watching how the crowded ones compete for space, light, water and nutrients and tend to grow weaker, thinner or smaller (real seedlings may instead grow tall and spindly).
Use the air toggle and consider air as a requirement too: plants need air as well as animals.
activities.intendedInsight: Different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements because they are suited to different homes — so 'more is always better' is false, and 'room to grow' and air are real needs alongside water and light.

activities.title: Match each plant to the conditions it likes
feedback: If a learner gives every plant the same water amount, revisit the compare-lab outcome: the cactus suffered with the fern's amount of water.

If a learner cannot connect thick, waxy leaves to low water needs, link back to the desert home where little water is available: thick, fleshy leaves can store water and a waxy coating helps stop water escaping, so these features often (though not always) suggest a plant that needs little water.
Reward answers that both name the five requirements AND tie differing amounts to the plant's habitat, in the learner's own words.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising, and choosing a suitable amount check the five requirements and the varies-plant-to-plant idea, and connect 'requirements vary' to habitat without over-reaching. These tasks confirm and consolidate the comparative understanding; recognition/matching alone checks rather than builds it and does not by itself elicit a learner's own explanation, so pair them with observation and ask for the 'why'.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the requirements of plants for life and growth (air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow) and how they vary from plant to plant'.
learnerActions: Match plants to their preferred conditions (e.g. cactus → dry/bright; fern → damp/shady), explaining each choice.
Name the five requirements — air, light, water, nutrients, and room — naming especially the ones people forget (air and room).
Decide how much water suits THIS plant: pick a suitable amount for a cactus versus a fern, rather than one amount for all plants.
Given a plant with thick, waxy leaves, infer what you would guess about how much water it needs, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: A plant thrives where its needs are met; reading a plant's features helps you predict the conditions it prefers, which shows that requirements vary from plant to plant.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: water both plants generously
feedback: A full response says the cactus struggles with lots of water (its roots rot; it is adapted to little), the fern is fine with plenty, AND generalises that needs vary in amount because plants suit different homes.
A partial response names variation and most of the five requirements but cannot explain WHY the cactus suffers or tie variation to habitat — prompt them to connect the plant to its home.

If a learner predicts both thrive, treat it as the 'more is always better' misconception and show the over-watered cactus outcome (an expected tendency with living plants, deterministic in the compare-lab).
activities.rationale: Over-watering both plants is the discriminator: only a child who knows a desert plant's needs predicts the cactus suffers. The pre-observation prediction separates genuine understanding of varying needs from the 'more is better' or 'all plants are the same' models.
sourceClaims: DfE Y3 statutory: 'explore the requirements of plants for life and growth (air, light, water, nutrients from soil, and room to grow) and how they vary from plant to plant'.
Children routinely omit air and room-to-grow from plant needs and treat soil nutrients as the plant's food; instruction should name the full set and keep 'nutrients from soil' as minerals-for-health.
learnerActions: Before observing, predict which of a cactus and a fern will thrive and which will struggle when BOTH are watered equally and generously for a fortnight — and say WHY.
Observe over the fortnight and record what actually happens to each plant.
Explain the result: why the same generous watering hurts a cactus but suits a fern.
Answer probe questions: What happens if you plant twenty seeds crammed in one tiny pot — which need runs short? Which of the five things do people most often forget?
activities.intendedInsight: The pre-observation reasoning is the key part: a child who understands that needs vary by plant predicts the cactus suffers from over-watering, while a 'more water is better' model wrongly predicts both thrive.

constraints: 'Nutrients from soil' means minerals for health, NOT the plant's food or the source of its mass; avoid letting this harden into 'plants eat soil', so the later 'plants make their own food from air and water' idea stays open.
More of a requirement is not always better: over-watering and excess fertiliser can harm, and the right amount differs by plant.

A static comparison poster (tap the cactus → 'little water, lots of light'; tap the fern → 'lots of water, shade'; tap the 'room' and 'air' icons) names the new factors and is a useful reference, but it does not let the child run the comparisons; use it to support, not replace, observation.

Matching, multiple-choice and slider tasks primarily check and consolidate understanding and may not by themselves build the comparative understanding or elicit a learner's own explanation; pair them with growth observation and ask for the 'why'.
Link 'requirements vary' to habitat (a plant thrives where its needs are met) to seed adaptation, without over-claiming more than the evidence supports at this stage.
Recognition and matching responses do not by themselves elicit independent explanation; ask learners to construct the 'why' in their own words.

Real-plant demonstrations (e.g. over-watering a cactus) are expected tendencies dependent on plant health, timing and conditions, not guaranteed results; the simulated compare-lab outcome is deterministic by design.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One source (OU OpenLearn §2.3) is marked verified:false in the row; treat its claim about children omitting air/room and misreading soil nutrients as unconfirmed.

The original artefact notes asserted that dialogue 'would displace the comparison' and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established facts, and have been dropped. A discussion or 3D model could still support learning; the proposal simply favours observable side-by-side comparison for this objective.

Practical caution: real over-watering/rotting demonstrations take time and depend on actual plant health and watering amounts; outcomes with living plants are expected tendencies, not guaranteed, and should be framed that way to learners.

The Y2-carryover misconception 'light is optional if the plant is watered' from the source pedagogy is not explicitly tackled in an activity; it is only implicitly covered by naming light among the five requirements. Consider adding an explicit check if desired.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: water a cactus and a fern equally and generously for a fortnight. Ask the child to predict which thrives and which struggles, and WHY, before observing. A 'more water is better' model predicts both thrive. The cactus suffers/rots. The pre-observation reasoning about differing needs is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Why would too much water hurt a cactus but not a fern?
Name the five things plants need to thrive — which ones do people forget?
What happens if you plant twenty seeds crammed in one tiny pot? Which need runs short?
If you found a plant with thick waxy leaves, what would you guess about how much water it needs?
assess.correctAnswer: The CACTUS struggles with lots of water — it's adapted to little water and its roots rot if over-watered; the fern is fine with plenty. Different plants need different AMOUNTS of the same requirements (air, light, water, nutrients, space) because they're suited to different homes. Full marks say the cactus suffers from too much water AND generalise that needs vary between plants.

errorPatterns.pattern: more water/light is always better for any plant
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a waterlogged cactus rotting — the right AMOUNT matters, and it differs by plant. More isn't always better.
errorPatterns.distractor: Both will thrive, because more water is always good for plants.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: predicts both plants thrive with lots of water, or that the cactus loves extra water

errorPatterns.pattern: all plants need exactly the same things in the same amounts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare desert vs forest homes — the plants are suited to different conditions, so their needs differ in amount.
errorPatterns.distractor: They need the same amount, because all plants are the same really.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: denies that a cactus and a fern differ in what they need

errorPatterns.pattern: 'room to grow' and air aren't real needs (only water and light count)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Crowd seedlings in one pot — they compete and stay small; space and nutrients are needs too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: lists only water/light; omits nutrients, air, space

responseLevels.gap: Thinks more water/light is always better, or all plants need identical amounts; lists only water and light.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the over-watered cactus struggles, explains needs vary in amount because plants are suited to different habitats, names all five requirements (air, light, water, nutrients, space), and reads a plant's features to infer its needs.
responseLevels.partial: Says needs can vary and names most of the five requirements, but can't explain WHY the cactus suffers or ties variation to habitat — the list without the matched-to-home reasoning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A cactus from the desert and a leafy fern from the forest floor are grown side by side, and I water BOTH of them a lot every single day. One thrives and one struggles. Which struggles — and the important part, why do two plants not need the same amount of the same things?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who understands needs vary by plant (matched to habitat) from one who thinks 'more is always better' or 'all plants need the same'. Over-watering both is the discriminator — only a child who knows a desert plant's needs predicts the cactus suffers.
